claim: Fixed idle-timeout watchdog unconditionally destroys the SSE stream after N seconds of silence, killing healthy connections when the model legitimately buffers a large payload before flushing (confirmed real by a same-day revert).
raw: The fixed idle-timeout watchdog treats "no bytes for N seconds" as "connection is dead" and unconditionally destroys the stream — which kills healthy connections when the model server legitimately buffers a large payload before flushing.

claim: Candidate event-loop race in the timer callback — the callback could false-fire and destroy a stream even when a chunk is ready — filtered/rejected as a likely false positive (score 25).
raw: **2. Event-loop race in the timer callback — score 25.** The claim was that the callback could false-fire even when a chunk is ready. This does not hold up: `clearTimer()` runs synchronously right after `await iterator.next()` resolves... Rejected as a likely false positive.

claim: Hard-coded 120s/60s idle timeouts call stream.destroy() on any long gap, killing healthy streams during known model tool-argument buffering pauses (confirmed by revert #308779 fixing #308627).
raw: Issue 1 (critical, confirmed by revert): Fixed 60s/120s idle timeouts kill healthy streams during known model-buffering pauses ... unconditionally calls `stream.destroy()` when it fires, treating "no chunk delivered within N ms" as equivalent to "connection is dead."

claim: Structural mismatch: a hard, provider-agnostic timeout that destroys the stream with no idleness re-check (the event-loop-race pattern) is a known-bad approach — the same failure recurred and was reverted in later PR #321671.
raw: The exact same structural weakness exists in `withStreamIdleTimeout` here: the timer is armed via `setTimeout` and fires unconditionally in its callback ... with no re-check of whether a chunk has actually just arrived ... precisely the "false-trigger due to event-loop timing" pattern the later reviewer called out.

claim: New streamIdleTimeout.spec.ts tests all use vi.useFakeTimers(), so they cannot exercise the real event-loop scheduling race between socket data-ready callbacks and timer callbacks under load.
raw: The unit tests added in `streamIdleTimeout.spec.ts` all use `vi.useFakeTimers()`, so they cannot exercise this real-event-loop race at all — they only validate the logical timer/next() ordering, not actual scheduling races between socket data-ready callbacks and timer callbacks under load.

claim: The idle-timeout watchdog destroys valid streams; confirmed by the author's same-day revert of a reported failure mode (score 75).
raw: The PR was reverted within hours of merge by its own author, addressing a reported failure mode where timeouts were destroying valid streams. This strongly indicates a real, serious issue in practice.

claim: PR reintroduces the previously-reverted withStreamIdleTimeout with identical timeout values and destroy-on-timeout mechanism, with no accommodation for the model-buffering scenario that caused the earlier revert.
raw: this is a re-run of a change that was already tried and reverted. ... The current diff reintroduces `withStreamIdleTimeout` in `fetcherService.ts` with the exact same `SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS`/`SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` values and destroy-on-timeout mechanism as the reverted version, with no visible accommodation for that buffering scenario.

claim: Timer callback calls stream.destroy() unconditionally with no explicit idleness re-check — scored 25 and rejected as a likely false positive (microtask clearTimer wins the race).
raw: The issue correctly identifies an unconditional `stream.destroy()` call in the setTimeout callback without explicit idleness re-check. However, the counter-argument is technically sound... SCORE: 25
